summary: Gives recommendations for jittering, or randomly adjusting, control message timing in mobile ad hoc network routing protocols, to reduce collisions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If everyone talks at exactly the same moment, no one hears anyone. Adding a little randomness to when they speak helps.

questions: why add random delay in manet routing
what is jitter in manet protocols
why add random delay to manet messages
subtitle: Add a little randomness to when wireless routers send control messages, so neighbours stop talking over each other.

tldr.problem: In a wireless network, nearby nodes that transmit at the same moment cause collisions, and scheduled, event-triggered and forwarded messages all tend to line nodes up in time.
tldr.mechanism: Nodes apply jitter, a random timing change bounded by a parameter called MAXJITTER: periodic messages are sent a random amount early, while triggered and forwarded messages are delayed by a random amount.
tldr.outcome: The recommendations reduce the chance of simultaneous transmissions and break them up if they happen. This is an informational document, and each protocol must define its own precise use of jitter.

today: RFC 5148 is an Informational document published in February 2008. The unit metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: Why Simultaneous Transmissions Hurt
sections.content:
In a wireless network, two nearby nodes sending at the same time can collide, so a receiver may fail to get some or all of the packets. Depending on the lower layers, the result is at best extra delay and at worst complete packet loss. Some of this can be fixed in lower layers, but sometimes the network layer and above must help.

RFC 5148 describes four features that make the problem worse: regularly scheduled messages, event-triggered messages, schedule reset after a triggered message, and forwarding. In each case, nearby nodes tend to act at the same moment, and then keep doing so.
sections.eli5: When neighbours all talk at once on a walkie-talkie, the message gets lost. Some habits, like everyone answering the same news right away, make it happen again and again.

sections.title: Where the Recommendations Apply
sections.content:
The advice applies to control messages of any MANET (Mobile Ad hoc NETwork) protocol where simultaneous transmissions are undesirable and where periodic, triggered or forwarded messages make them likely. Proactive protocols such as OLSR (RFC 3626) use scheduled messages, reactive protocols such as AODV (RFC 3561) use event-triggered ones, and both forward messages.

It is meant for cases where the medium access control and lower layers do not already avoid collisions effectively. Where they do, the recommendations are not needed. The document was generalized from the jitter mechanism of OLSR. Alternatives such as pseudo-random variation based on node identity are not discussed.
sections.eli5: The tip is for networks where radios can bump into each other. If the equipment already takes turns well, you do not need it.

sections.title: Three Jitter Mechanisms
sections.content:
Jitter, a deliberate random variation in timing, SHOULD be used in three cases, each with its own maximum, called MAXJITTER. A protocol MAY use the same or different values for each case and for each message type.

  • Periodic messages: jitter shortens the interval. The delay between messages of the same type is MESSAGE_INTERVAL - jitter. Subtracting means the interval never exceeds MESSAGE_INTERVAL, so timeouts are not harmed. Basing the next time on the previous transmission, not on a fixed clock, lets nodes become completely desynchronized.
  • Externally triggered messages: the message SHOULD be delayed by a random duration. If periodic messages are rescheduled, that is based on the delayed time.
  • Forwarded messages: forwarding SHOULD be delayed by a random duration.

In all three cases the random value SHOULD be generated uniformly between zero and MAXJITTER.
sections.eli5: Instead of speaking exactly on the beat, each kid speaks a tiny random bit early or late. Soon they are all out of step, so they stop talking over each other.

sections.title: Triggered Messages and Forwarding Details
sections.content:
A protocol MAY set a minimum gap between messages of the same type, MESSAGE_MIN_INTERVAL, which is zero if not required. The RFC allows this gap to be reduced by jitter too, so the next message is allowed after MESSAGE_MIN_INTERVAL - jitter. This looks odd, but in a very dynamic network triggers can arrive faster than the minimum interval, which then acts as the default interval, so it needs jitter to avoid synchronization.

If a triggered message is delayed by jitter and another trigger arrives while it waits, the right action is protocol specific, typically discarding the earlier message or sending both. The same holds for forwarding when a node receives a message while still waiting to forward an earlier one from the same originator.

When several messages arrive in one packet, they SHOULD be forwarded in a single packet, so they SHOULD share the same jitter. One random value must be chosen for all of them. Giving each its own value and taking the smallest would produce a non-uniform distribution with a reduced mean.
sections.eli5: If a second reason to speak shows up while you are waiting your turn, the rules say to decide per game whether to drop the old note or send both. When a group of notes travels together, they wait one shared random time.

sections.title: Choosing MAXJITTER
sections.content:
Jitter adds delay that usually hurts a well-designed protocol, so MAXJITTER SHOULD be minimized while still achieving its purpose. For periodic messages, it MUST NOT be negative, MUST NOT be greater than MESSAGE_INTERVAL/2, and SHOULD NOT be greater than MESSAGE_INTERVAL/4.

If MESSAGE_MIN_INTERVAL is above zero, MAXJITTER MUST NOT be greater than it and SHOULD NOT be greater than half of it. It should also suit the lower layers: significantly greater, for example an order of magnitude, than any medium access control frame period.

Greater jitter is appropriate when collisions are more likely, in particular with increased node density. When forwarding, the choice MAY take into account how many times a message may be forwarded in turn, up to the network diameter in hops, so that the accumulated delay is bounded. A forwarding node does not automatically know the originator's MESSAGE_INTERVAL, so this may need prior agreement, inclusion in the message, or estimation.
sections.eli5: Wait only as long as you need to. A short random wait is enough in a quiet room, and a longer one helps in a crowded room, but never so long that you miss your turn.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document gives recommendations for mechanisms, and full security considerations are left to the protocols that use them. It does note one possible benefit: random timing makes it harder to predict transmission times, and so harder for an attacker to jam selectively by scheduling jamming transmissions to coincide with protocol messages.
sections.eli5: If you never speak at the same moment twice, a troublemaker cannot easily time their noise to drown you out.

items.title: Periodic generation
items.text: Reduce the interval: MESSAGE_INTERVAL minus a random jitter.

items.title: Externally triggered
items.text: Delay the message by a random amount.

items.title: Forwarding
items.text: Delay the forwarded message by a random amount.
